title: Inspecting Git Objects
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundaries of inspecting git objects.
Choose and interpret a Git command relevant to inspecting git objects using a disposable repository.
Verify the result with repository state or history and identify one safety limitation.

content.intro: This lesson introduces inspecting git objects as part of Git Internals and Object Storage. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: `git cat-file` reads stored Git objects by type or ID. It is a useful low-level inspection tool for learning how commits refer to trees and blobs without editing repository internals.

content_blocks.title: Git object model
content_blocks.alt_text: A blob stores file content, a tree stores directory entries and modes, a commit points to a tree and parent commit(s), and refs name commits or other objects.
content_blocks.caption: Original CodeLeaf diagram. Review labels as well as the explanatory text; color is not the only signal.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** `git cat-file` reads stored Git objects by type or ID. It is a useful low-level inspection tool for learning how commits refer to trees and blobs without editing repository internals.

For **Inspecting Git Objects**, keep the named subtopics in view: Using git cat-file; Examining object types; Inspecting object content; Understanding object identifiers. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Use a repository with at least one commit. Plumbing commands expose lower-level structures; use them read-only unless a task explicitly calls for object creation.

content_blocks.title: Command example: Inspecting Git Objects
content_blocks.code:
git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD
content_blocks.expected_output: The object type for HEAD (normally commit), followed by its stored commit object content.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a repository with at least one commit. Plumbing commands expose lower-level structures; use them read-only unless a task explicitly calls for object creation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a disposable repository. If the exercise changes state, check git status and git log before and after; discard the practice directory only after confirming it contains no valuable work.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf web lesson page does not execute arbitrary Git commands. Run commands locally in a disposable repository with a Git version appropriate to your task. Placeholder paths, branches, commit IDs and repository URLs must be replaced with values from that practice repository.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

task: Inspect one repository object or reference using read-only plumbing commands. Record the object type and explain how it relates to the working tree, index, or commit graph.
hints: Start by reviewing: Using git cat-file.
Use a read-only inspection command before any operation that changes files, refs or remote state.
After the example, verify with git status --short --branch and/or git log --oneline --graph as appropriate.
expected_output: The object type for HEAD (normally commit), followed by its stored commit object content.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
